883.title: The stone Buddhas
883.hook: at Gal Vihara in Polonnaruwa, great Buddhas carved from one rock, standing, seated, lying
883.howItsDone: Pilgrims at Gal Vihara remove their shoes, offer flowers and sit or stand quietly before the figures; in Buddhist temples, seated and reclining images serve as a focus for meditation and devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddhaghosa arrived and built a whole book on one verse. Your line was the commentator. Did you read one line slowly? Today, the teaching in stone instead of words. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

A long face of granite, in the old royal city of Polonnaruwa in Sri Lanka. Out of it, sculptors cut the Buddha: seated in meditation, standing with arms folded, and lying on his side. Nothing was carried in and set in place. The figures were uncovered, the stone around them cut away, so that each one is still part of the hill. The place is called Gal Vihara, the rock monastery.
screen: `ONE FACE OF GRANITE.` → `SEATED, STANDING, LYING.` → `GAL VIHARA.`

segments.voice: First, the place. The later chronicle credits King Parakramabahu with rebuilding Polonnaruwa as a royal city of parks, reservoirs and monasteries, and with the rock monastery itself. Second, the seated Buddha. He sits in meditation, hands resting in his lap, with a calm the stone holds without effort. Behind him the rock is carved with small details, as if he sits in a shrine of his own. Third, the standing figure, arms folded across his chest. Who is he? People disagree. Some say the Buddha himself, in the days after his awakening. Others say Ananda, his companion and attendant, standing in grief beside his dying teacher. The stone doesn't say, and the debate is still open. Fourth, the lying Buddha. In the account of the Buddha's last days, the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, he lies down on his right side, one foot resting on the other, mindful and clear, between two sal trees. The great reclining figure lies just that way, his head on a pillow. Some see a sleeping Buddha. Others see the final passing. The chronicle doesn't say why the sculptors chose to work in a single rock. What the stone itself shows is simple: nothing is stacked or joined. The figures share one body with the hill. And a stone Buddha does not fidget, does not check the time, does not shift its weight. Part of what people come for is to sit near that stillness for a while.
screen: `A KING'S ROCK MONASTERY.` · `SEATED, IN MEDITATION.` · `STANDING: THE BUDDHA, OR ANANDA?` · `LYING ON HIS RIGHT SIDE.` · then, large: `CARVED FROM ONE ROCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit like a stone Buddha. Find a steady seat, on a chair or on the floor. Let your hands rest in your lap. Let your back be upright without strain, the way stone is upright without trying. Now, for the length of the bell, try not to adjust. When an itch comes, or the urge to shift, notice it, and see whether it can pass the way weather passes over rock. If you need to move, move gently, and settle again. The bell holds the time.
Gal Vihara. The rock monastery at Polonnaruwa where the Buddha was cut seated, standing and lying from a single face of granite. Today's word.
Your line: carved from one rock. Today, once, when you want to fidget or reach for your phone, stay still for a few breaths, like stone. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

on his right side, one foot resting on the other.

fork.reveal: the Mahaparinibbana Sutta says he lay on his right side, one foot on the other, mindful and clear. the reclining figure at Gal Vihara lies the same way.

original.note: Pali: parinibbana, the Buddha's final passing, which the reclining figure is often read to show.

trapdoor: what you thought: separate statues set side by side.
what it means: figures cut from one face of granite: seated, standing and lying.
what a scholar hears: the later chronicle credits King Parakramabahu, and the standing figure is still debated: the Buddha, or Ananda in grief.

884.title: The tooth relic
884.hook: the Buddha's tooth relic, guarded in Kandy
884.howItsDone: At the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, monks hold rituals for the relic and pilgrims offer flowers and incense, and the Esala Perahera procession carries a relic casket through the city's streets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gal Vihara's stone Buddhas. Your line was carved from one rock. Did you stay still like stone for a few breaths? Today, something very small that kings guarded. Day eight hundred eighty-four.

After the Buddha's cremation, the Mahaparinibbana Sutta says, his relics nearly started a war. Kings and clans arrived from all sides, each demanding a share. Then a brahmin named Dona spoke up. The Buddha taught patience, he reminded them; it would not be right to come to blows over the remains of such a teacher. So the relics were divided, and each share went home to be honored in a stupa. Sri Lankan tradition says one tooth took a longer road, and it ends in a temple in Kandy.
screen: `THE RELICS NEARLY START A WAR.` → `DONA: HE TAUGHT PATIENCE.` → `ONE TOOTH, A LONGER ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the journey. The chronicle of the tooth, the Dathavamsa, tells how the tooth was kept in India and then, in a time of danger, sent across the sea. A princess named Hemamala and a prince named Dantha, the story says, carried it to Sri Lanka hidden in her hair. Second, the guarding. On the island, the tooth became bound up with kingship. The chronicles describe kings building shrines for it near their palaces and taking it with them when the capital moved. Whoever kept the tooth safe, tradition held, had a claim to rule. Third, Kandy. The relic is kept today in the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, the Sri Dalada Maligawa. Monks perform rituals for it, and pilgrims bring flowers. The tooth itself rests inside nested caskets and is not usually shown. People honor what they cannot see. Fourth, the procession. In the festival called the Esala Perahera, a casket representing the relic is carried through the streets of Kandy on an elephant, with drummers and dancers all around. What does honoring a relic mean? Buddhists explain it in different ways: a reminder of the Buddha, a focus for devotion, a link to a real person who walked and taught. And the sutta's own scene is worth keeping in mind. The Buddha's remains almost started a fight, and it was a reminder of his teaching on patience that stopped it.
screen: `CARRIED IN A PRINCESS'S HAIR.` · `GUARDED BY KINGS.` · `KEPT IN KANDY, UNSEEN.` · `CARRIED THROUGH THE STREETS.` · then, large: `KEPT SAFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one precious thing. Let your shoulders drop, and breathe out slowly. Bring to mind something precious to you. Not expensive, precious: a grandparent's ring, a child's drawing, an old letter, a photograph. If it's nearby, you can hold it. If not, picture it clearly. Remember who gave it, or what it holds. With each breath, simply honor it, the way pilgrims in Kandy bring flowers to a casket they never see opened. The bell holds the time.
Datha. The tooth, carried to Sri Lanka hidden in a princess's hair, and guarded today in the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy. Today's word.
Your line: kept safe. Today, give one precious thing a safe place, somewhere worthy of it. Day eight hundred eighty-four.

fork.reveal: Dona reminded them the Buddha taught patience, and the relics were shared out, each portion honored in a stupa.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old object in a museum case.
what it means: a relic honored with daily devotion and guarded across the generations.
what a scholar hears: in Sri Lanka, keeping the tooth was tied to the right to rule, and the Dathavamsa tells its journey from India.

885.title: Bagan
885.hook: thousands of temples on the plain of Bagan in Myanmar
885.howItsDone: Buddhists in Myanmar visit the temples of Bagan to offer flowers, candles and food, walk barefoot through the shrines, and dedicate the merit of their giving to their families and to all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, datha, the tooth relic, carried across the sea and guarded in Kandy. Your line was kept safe. Did you give something precious a safe place? Today we travel east, to Myanmar. Day eight hundred eighty-five.

Dawn, on a wide dry plain beside the Irrawaddy River in Myanmar. As the mist thins, shapes rise out of it: temples and stupas of red brick and white plaster, some enormous, some no bigger than a garden shed, scattered in every direction as far as the eye can reach. The plain is quiet, except for a bell somewhere, a broom on a step, a few early visitors taking off their sandals at a doorway. The donors who paid for these buildings called them gifts, and some carved their wishes in stone.
screen: `DAWN BESIDE THE IRRAWADDY.` → `TEMPLES AS FAR AS THE EYE CAN SEE.` → `BAGAN.`

segments.voice: First, the king and the monk. The Burmese chronicles tell how King Anawrahta of Bagan met a monk named Shin Arahan, who taught him the Theravada teaching. They go on to say the king wanted the scriptures and monks of Thaton, a kingdom to the south, and when its king refused him, he went to war and brought them back. Historians question parts of that story, but it is how the tradition remembers Bagan's beginning. Second, building as giving. Over generations, kings, queens, officials and ordinary families built on the plain. In Buddhist teaching, generous giving makes merit, good that ripens in this life and in lives to come, and a temple was a great gift to make. Inscriptions left by donors survive, and some record their wishes: to meet a future Buddha, to reach nibbana, to share the merit with their parents and with all beings. Third, the inside. Some temples are not solid mounds at all. You can walk into them, through dim corridors painted with scenes from the Buddha's past lives, past rows of seated Buddhas lit by small windows. Fourth, the plain today. Earthquakes have shaken Bagan, and some temples have cracked, fallen or been rebuilt. It is still a place of devotion: people come to make offerings, light candles and walk barefoot through the corridors. A plain of temples is what happens when people, over a long time, each decide to give something that will outlast them.
screen: `A KING, A MONK, A WAR.` · `EACH TEMPLE A GIFT.` · `PAINTED CORRIDORS INSIDE.` · `SHAKEN, REBUILT, STILL VISITED.` · then, large: `A PLAIN OF TEMPLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the plain of temples. Close your eyes or soften your gaze. See the plain at dawn: mist, flat dry ground, temples rising out of it, near and far. Now choose one small temple. Picture the people who built it. Not a king, maybe a family, putting what they could spare into bricks. Breathe with that picture. On each out-breath, let a good wish go out from you, as the donors did, toward someone you love, or toward everyone. The bell holds the time.
Bagan. The plain beside the Irrawaddy in Myanmar, where kings and ordinary families built temples and stupas, gift after gift. Today's word.
Your line: a plain of temples. Today, give one small thing that might outlast the day: some time, a kind word, a hand with something heavy. Day eight hundred eighty-five.

886.title: Shwedagon
886.hook: the golden stupa of Yangon, said to hold hairs of the Buddha
886.howItsDone: Visitors to the Shwedagon climb barefoot, walk clockwise around the stupa, offer flowers, candles and gold leaf, and pour water over the Buddha image at the shrine for the day of the week they were born.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bagan. Your line was a plain of temples. Did you give one small thing that might outlast the day? Today, a single stupa in Yangon, covered in gold. Day eight hundred eighty-six.

Shoes off at the bottom of the stairs. Everyone climbs barefoot. At the top, a wide platform opens out around a great golden stupa, shaped like a bell, narrowing to a spire, blazing in the afternoon sun and ringed by smaller shrines. People walk around it slowly, clockwise. Some sit to meditate. Some chant. Some pour water over a small Buddha image at a corner shrine. This is the Shwedagon, in Yangon.
screen: `SHOES OFF, CLIMB BAREFOOT.` → `A GOLDEN BELL AGAINST THE SKY.` → `THE SHWEDAGON.`

segments.voice: First, the story. The Vinaya tells of two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, who meet the Buddha soon after his awakening, offer him food, and become his first lay followers. Later tradition adds what the Vinaya doesn't say: the Buddha gave them hairs from his head. Burmese tradition says they carried them home, where the hairs were enshrined on a hill. That hill is where the Shwedagon stands. Second, the gold. The stupa is covered in gold, given over generations by rulers and ordinary people; tradition at the site remembers a queen who gave her own weight in gold. Visitors still bring small squares of gold leaf and press them onto Buddha images. The shine is made of gifts. Third, the corners. Around the base are shrines for the days of the week, by the Burmese way of counting them. People go to the shrine for the day they were born, pour water over the Buddha image there, and make offerings. So each person on the platform brings something of their own to it: their birthday, their family's wishes, their troubles. Fourth, the stupa itself. Like the stupas of Sanchi, it is a reliquary, a mound built around something precious, and walking around it clockwise, keeping it on the right, is a way of honoring what is inside. Nobody sees the hairs. As at Kandy, people honor what they cannot see, and what they bring is gold, water, flowers, and the simple act of walking around.
screen: `THE MERCHANTS AND THE HAIRS.` · `GOLD, GIVEN BY MANY HANDS.` · `A SHRINE FOR YOUR BIRTH DAY.` · `WALK AROUND, KEEP IT ON THE RIGHT.` · then, large: `THE GOLDEN STUPA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture a golden stupa. Sit comfortably, eyes lowered or closed. Feel a warm stone platform under bare feet. Ahead of you, a golden stupa, wide at the base, narrowing to a point against the sky. Now picture yourself walking slowly around it, clockwise, keeping it on your right. Let each breath be a step. At the center, let there be whatever you most want to honor. Just keep circling it, gently, breath by breath. If you pray, you can bring a line you already know. The bell holds the time.
Shwedagon. The golden stupa of Yangon, said by Burmese tradition to hold hairs of the Buddha, circled by barefoot pilgrims. Today's word.
Your line: the golden stupa. Today, walk once, slowly and on purpose, around something you care about: a room, a garden, a block. Day eight hundred eighty-six.

887.title: Sukhothai
887.hook: the Thai kingdom whose walking Buddha images seem to move
887.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, monks and lay meditators often practice walking meditation, pacing slowly along a short path, and walking Buddha images in the Sukhothai style are still made and honored in Thailand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shwedagon in Yangon, which tradition says holds hairs of the Buddha. Your line was the golden stupa. When you pictured it, what did you see first, the gold or the people walking around it? Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

A bronze figure, caught mid-stride. The right heel is just lifting off the ground. One hand is raised, palm out. The body leans a little, the way a body leans when it is really walking and not posing for anyone. The robe clings to the legs as if a breeze had caught it. This week we've already met Buddhas carved in rock, sitting, standing and lying down. This one is going somewhere. Sculptors in an old Thai kingdom made images like this, and people who stand in front of them say the bronze seems to move. So where is he walking, and why would anyone cast a Buddha in motion? Today, the kingdom of the walking Buddha.
screen: `A BRONZE BUDDHA, MID-STRIDE.` → `THE HEEL IS LIFTING.` → `WHERE IS HE GOING?`

segments.voice: First, the place. Sukhothai is the name of a kingdom and its old capital, in what is now Thailand. Its ruins still stand among trees and ponds: brick temple platforms, stupas, and rows of seated Buddhas, with the walking ones among them. Its kings supported Theravada monks, the same stream of teaching we followed to Sri Lanka and Myanmar. Second, the story people see in the stride. Tradition tells that the Buddha once spent a rainy season in Tavatimsa heaven, teaching his mother, who had died soon after his birth. When the season ended, he came back down to earth by a stairway, with crowds waiting at the bottom. Some readers see that very moment in the walking image: the Buddha stepping down to meet people again. Third, walking was practice, not just travel. In the old suttas, monks pace back and forth on a short path, and the Buddha walks it too. The Pali word is cankama, walking up and down. One discourse praises it in plain terms: it helps you bear long journeys, it helps your food digest, and the calm you find while walking tends to last. Fourth, the face. Look at it on a walking Buddha and it is not hurrying. The body moves; the face stays quiet. That's the picture the sculptors left behind: a mind that can stay still while the feet keep going. A day is full of moving, from the bed to the kettle, from the door to the bus. Sukhothai's bronze makes a claim about all of it: calm doesn't wait for you to sit down.
screen: `SUKHOTHAI: AN OLD THAI KINGDOM.` · `STEPPING DOWN FROM TAVATIMSA HEAVEN.` · `CANKAMA: WALKING AS PRACTICE.` · `A QUIET FACE ON A MOVING BODY.` · then, large: `THE WALKING BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk slowly and gracefully. If you can, stand up and find a few steps of clear floor. If you can't walk right now, rest your hands on your knees and do it in your mind. Lift one heel, slowly, and feel the weight roll forward. Let the foot touch down. Then the other. At the end of your short path, pause, turn, and come back. Let the arms hang loose. Let the face go soft, like the bronze. No need to get anywhere. The bell holds the time.
Sukhothai. The old Thai kingdom whose sculptors cast the Buddha walking, heel lifting, face at rest. Today's word.
Your line: the walking Buddha. Today, pick one short walk, from the sink to the table or the door to the car, and take it slowly, with a soft face. Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

walking up and down as practice

fork.reveal: Sukhothai's sculptors cast him walking. the body moves, but the face stays quiet, and tradition links the stride to his return from Tavatimsa heaven.

original.note: Pali: walking up and down, the walking practice monks do in the suttas.

888.title: Angkor
888.hook: Jayavarman VII, a Buddhist king of Cambodia, and the smiling faces of the Bayon
888.howItsDone: Cambodian Buddhists and visitors from many places come to the Bayon at Angkor Thom, and in Mahayana Buddhism Avalokiteshvara is honored as the bodhisattva of compassion, often called on in chant and prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukhothai, the Thai kingdom that cast the Buddha mid-stride. Your line was the walking Buddha. Did you take one short walk slowly, and did your face stay soft the whole way? Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

Climb the steep stone steps of the Bayon, at the heart of the old city of Angkor Thom in Cambodia, and the faces find you before you find them. A great stone face on a tower, eyes half closed, lips turned up at the corners. Turn your head, and there's another, looking off in a different direction. Then another, on the next tower over. Moss in the cracks, lichen on the cheeks, and still that same calm, closed-mouth smile. Wherever you stand on the upper terrace, someone made of stone seems to be quietly smiling. Visitors have argued for a long time about whose face it is. Today, the king who built it, and what the smile might mean.
screen: `THE STEPS OF THE BAYON.` → `A FACE ON EVERY TOWER.` → `WHOSE FACE IS IT?`

segments.voice: First, the king. Angkor was the seat of a great Khmer kingdom, and kings there had built huge temples, some of them for Hindu gods, like Vishnu at Angkor Wat. King Jayavarman the Seventh was a Buddhist, of the Mahayana stream, and when he built his walled city he put the Bayon at its center. Second, the question nobody can settle. The temple left no label on the faces. Some scholars see the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, called Lokeshvara in Cambodia. Some see the king himself. Some see both at once: a ruler who wanted to be seen as compassion turned in every direction. The honest answer is that we don't know, and the stone doesn't say. Third, the bodhisattva behind the guess. In the Lotus Sutra, Avalokiteshvara is the one who hears beings who call out in trouble and comes to help, taking whatever form will reach them. A face turned to every point of the compass fits that picture well. Fourth, what the king's own words add. Inscriptions from his reign tell of hospitals and rest houses he founded, and one hospital inscription says, in substance, that the suffering of his people was his own pain. A king can say beautiful things, of course, and historians weigh them carefully. But it is the same idea as the towers: a face that doesn't look away. And the smile itself? It isn't laughing at anything. It isn't a grin for a camera. It's the kind of smile that has nowhere in particular to point, gentle, a little inward, offered to whoever happens to be standing there.
screen: `JAYAVARMAN VII, A BUDDHIST KING AT ANGKOR.` · `WHOSE FACES? NOBODY CAN SAY FOR SURE.` · `LOKESHVARA HEARS THOSE WHO CALL.` · `THEIR SUFFERING WAS HIS PAIN.` · then, large: `THE SMILING TOWERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: smile gently at nothing. Sit comfortably and let your eyes half close, like the faces on the towers. Let the corners of your mouth lift, just slightly. Not a grin. Not for anyone. Notice what happens around the eyes, in the jaw, in the shoulders. Breathe in, and keep the small smile. Breathe out, and keep it. If it fades, let it return without fuss. If it feels strange, that's fine too. Just notice. The bell holds the time.
Angkor. The old Khmer capital in Cambodia, where King Jayavarman the Seventh raised the Bayon and its towers of quiet, smiling faces. Today's word.
Your line: the smiling towers. Today, once, when someone crosses your path, let your face rest in that small smile, asking nothing back. Day eight hundred eighty-eight.

one guess for whose faces they are
his people's suffering was his pain

889.title: Luang Prabang's dawn
889.hook: the daily alms round in Laos, monks in a long saffron line
889.howItsDone: In Laos and other Theravada countries, monks walk an alms round early in the morning, and lay people kneel or stand by the road to place rice and other food in their bowls, often in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the smiling towers of Angkor. This week we traveled: Buddhas carved from one rock, a tooth relic kept safe, a plain of temples, a golden stupa, a walking Buddha, and stone faces smiling every way. Which place stayed with you? Today, people instead of stone. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.

It's still dark in the old town of Luang Prabang, in Laos. The street is quiet. Along the curb, people kneel on small mats, shoes off, a covered basket of warm sticky rice beside each of them. Then, from down the road, a line of monks appears, walking barefoot, single file, in saffron robes, each with a bowl held in front. Nobody calls out. Nobody bargains. A monk pauses for a breath at each person, the lid of the bowl lifts, a small ball of rice goes in, and the line moves on. By the time the sky turns pale, it's over. Today, the line at dawn, and what is really being exchanged.

segments.voice: First, the name for it. In Pali it's pindapata, the alms round: walking for food that is given. Monks in the Theravada tradition receive their meals from lay people rather than buying them, so this walk is not a show put on for the morning. It is how the monastery eats. Second, the bowl takes what is given. A monk on alms round doesn't ask, point, or choose. He stands, receives, and walks on. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, has a picture for this: "As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village." Take a little, harm nothing, move along. Third, giving goes both ways. The person on the mat is practicing too. Giving is called dana, and the Buddha taught it to lay people as a practice in its own right. A short discourse in the Itivuttaka says householders support monks with robes, food and shelter, and monks support householders with the teaching, so each holds the other up. The rice goes into the bowl; the teaching comes back out of the monastery. Fourth, guests at the edge. The alms round now draws visitors with cameras too. Local monks and community leaders have asked visitors to keep a respectful distance, stay quiet, and not give unless they mean it and know how. That request belongs to the lesson too: some things are only beautiful when nobody turns them into a spectacle.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the saffron line. Close your eyes and let it be just before dawn. A cool street. A mat under your knees. Warm rice in a basket. Hear bare feet coming down the road, almost silent. Watch one bowl stop in front of you. Notice what it's like simply to give, without a word, without thanks, without a photo. Then watch the line move on into the pale light. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Pindapata. The alms round in the old town of Laos: monks walking in a saffron line, people kneeling to give rice. Today's word.
Your line: the line at dawn. Today, give one small thing the way the rice is given: quietly, without asking for anything back. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.
